'''''Geranium sanguineum''''', [[common name]] '''bloody crane's-bill'''<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020>{{cite web |title=Bloody Crane's-bill ''Geranium sanguineum'' L. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5=D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |date=2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.xxz |access-date=22 June 2024 }}</ref><ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|accessdate=2014-10-17}}</ref> or '''bloody geranium''', is a [[species]] of [[hardiness (plants)|hardy]] flowering [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] in the cranesbill [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Geraniaceae]].<ref>{{GRIN | accessdate=15 July 2013}}</ref> It is the [[County flowers of the United Kingdom|county flower]] of [[Northumberland]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = Bloody crane's-bill {{!}} Plant & fungi species {{!}} Wild plants|url = http://www.plantlife.org.uk/wild_plants/plant_species/bloody_cranes-bill/|website = www.plantlife.org.uk| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160707153412/http://www.plantlife.org.uk/wild_plants/plant_species/bloody_cranes-bill/ |accessdate = 2016-01-03| archive-date=7 July 2016 }}</ref>

==Etymology==
The genus name is derived from the Greek γέρανος ("géranos"), meaning [[Crane (bird)|crane]], with reference to the fruit capsule resembling the bird's bill. The specific Latin name ''sanguineum'' means 'blood-red'; Linnaeus cites [[Gaspard Bauhin]]'s 1623 book ''Pinax theatri botanici'' as his source for the name, which in turn refers ("''sanguinaria radix''") to a blood-red root.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bauhin |first1=Gaspard |title=Pinax theatri botanici |date=1623 |publisher=Basileae Helvet. |page=318 |url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/viewer/10754/?offset=#page=342&viewer=picture&o=ocr&n=0&q=}}</ref>

==Description==
''Geranium sanguineum'' has a [[Raunkiær plant life-form#Hemicryptophytes|hemicryptophyte]] [[Raunkiær plant life-form|plant life-form]], with its overwintering buds situated just below the soil surface, and the [[floral axis]] more or less erect with a few leaves. It has a thick [[rhizome]]. The stems are prostrate to ascending, well developed, much branched, and hairy. It reaches on average {{convert|30|-|50|cm}} in height.<ref name=Pignatti>Pignatti S. - Flora d'Italia – Edagricole – 1982. Vol. II, pag. 6</ref> The [[Petiole (botany)|petiolate]] leaves have five lobes (or segments), each segment is tripartite with large teeth. The flowers are produced singly (not in clusters, as in many other ''Geranium'' species), 2.5–4 cm diameter, with petals 12–18 mm wide, and are bright crimson.<ref name = "Streeter">Streeter D, Hart-Davies C, Hardcastle A, Cole F, Harper L. 2009. ''Collins Flower Guide''. Harper Collins {{ISBN|9-78-000718389-0}}</ref> The flowering period extends from May to October. The flowers are [[Glossary of botanical terms|hermaphrodite]] and pollinated by insects ([[entomophily]]). The most common flower visitors are Syrphidae and Hymenoptera, but also butterflies and Coleoptera. The fruit is a [[Glossary of botanical terms#schizocarp|schizocarp]] that breaks up into five [[Glossary of botanical terms#mericarp|mericarps]] when ripe.<ref name=Pignatti/>

==Distribution==
''Geranium sanguineum'' is [[native plant|native]] to most of temperate to subarctic Europe and western Asia.<ref name="POWO">{{Cite POWO |last1=POWO |author-link1=Plants of the World Online |id=322494-2 |title=''Geranium sanguineum'' L. |access-date=22 June 2024 }}</ref> It is also frequent as a garden escape away from native sites.<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020 />

==Habitat==
It typically occurs in [[grassland]], being particularly abundant on [[sand dune ecology|coastal sand dunes]],<ref name="Swan">{{cite book |last1=Swan |first1=George A. |title=Flora of Northumberland |date=1993 |publisher=Natural History Society of Northumbria |location=Hancock Museum |isbn=0-9520782-0-1 |page=161 }}</ref> but also in open woodland on [[calcareous soil]]s, including rocky slopes. It prefers a neutral pH, with low nutritional value, at altitudes from {{convert|0|to|1200|m}} above sea level.<ref name=Pignatti/>
